## Milestone 02 !! Understanding the Dataset and Limits.

This UMD course data is similar to the one from the lab before. However the differences are shown in th amount of variables. There is only 7 columns in this UMD_COURSES. Section column and syllabus_count are absent from this data set, so this takes away some of the more statistical quantitative analysis that can be made. But the department, seats, descriptions, course title and professor name can provide enough of the questions.  

Also this specific data set only goes into the spring of 2023 and has missing semesters. Half of 2019 semesters are not provided which would make it hard to see trends. I would probably not work with the data before the gaps if I want to come up with sound conclusions. Also the data being a bit outdated limits some of the questions I provided, like the one about the "contemporary Trump Department of Education's" definition of professional. Although, this might prove some type of correlation between the reasoning stripping the professional label from certain majors and  the trend of those courses availability.On the other hand, I am not sure if that holds any relevance since this data is from nearly three years ago. 

Any of the questions that have to do with numbers will be fine.  




## Milestone 3-- :Analysis Questions and reflections 

**Q1**: Isolate the spring and fall semesters, calculate the total number of courses per instructor and the total amount of seats they've offered. Do per term/year in one dataframe then overall in another dataframe. What are the patterns and findings? Do a cor test to see if the number of seats offered is related to the number of courses taught to check whether instructors with more courses also tend to teach larger total seat counts. If no correlation, explain why 



A Pearson correlation was conducted to examine the relationship between the number of courses taught by each instructor and the total number of seats they offered. The correlation was statistically significant, r = .066, p < .001, however, it was a very weak positive relationship. The effect size is negligible because the correlation is almost close to zero at 0.66. This suggests that instructors who teach more courses do not meaningfully offer more seats. This is because a professor could teach many seminar classes that three registered students. Therefore, the amount of classes instructors teach at UMD appears to be driven by other independent variables such as employment status (lecturer, adjunct) and institutional policies.


```{r}
#finding total of courses taught by each professor from 2017 to 2025
instructor_counts_all_sems <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(instructors, sep = ";\\s*") |>
  mutate(instructors = trimws(instructors)) |>
  group_by(instructors) |>
  summarise(n_courses = n(), .groups = "drop") 

#output 
instructor_counts_all_sems

#Creating dataframe for each instructor and their department, decided not to join with instructor_counts because professors teach under multiple departments and instructor_counts is a total of all the classes they've taught, across departments, from 2017 to 2023. 

instructor_department_ref <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(instructors, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(instructors = trimws(instructors)) |>
  select(instructors, department) |>
  distinct()

#output
instructor_department_ref

#finding total of courses taught by each professor in the fall and spring terms from 2017 to 2023
courses_fall_spring <- umd_courses |>
  mutate(
    year = as.integer(substr(term, 1, 4)),
    sem_code = substr(term, 5, 6)
  ) %>%
  filter(
    year >= 2017, year <= 2025,
    sem_code %in% c("01", "08")
  ) %>%
  select(-year, -sem_code) 

#creating a column for standard semester dates 
courses_fall_spring <- courses_fall_spring |>
  mutate(
    term_code = as.character(term),
    year = str_sub(term_code, 1, 4),
    term_suffix = str_sub(term_code, 5, 6),
    start_date = case_when(
      term_suffix == "01" ~ ymd(paste0(year, "-01-24")),  # Spring
      term_suffix == "08" ~ ymd(paste0(year, "-08-26")),  # Fall
      TRUE ~ NA_Date_
    )) |>
  select(-term_code, -term_suffix, -year)



instructor_counts_fall_spring <- courses_fall_spring |>
  separate_rows(instructors, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(instructors = trimws(instructors)) |>
  group_by(instructors, term) |>
  summarise(n_courses = n(), 
            n_seats   = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop"
  )

instructor_total_major_semesters <- courses_fall_spring |>
  separate_rows(instructors, sep = ";\\s*") |>
  mutate(instructors = trimws(instructors)) |>
  group_by(instructors) |>
  summarise(n_courses = n(), 
            n_seats   = sum(seats, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(n_seats)) 

#OUTPUT 
instructor_total_major_semesters


#Can we make a graph to show the highest instructor 

```


```{r}

         instructor_total_major_semesters$n_seats)
```

**Q2**: Which departments had the least amount of professors across the years? which ones had the most? Are there any patterns in the results? 
  
 **A2**: The departments Business and Management and English had the most amount of professors for the spring and fall semesters between 2018 to 2023. Though Business and Management also had the highest number of seats across the observed semesters, the English department wider ratio of more professors than total seats per observed semester. 

```{r}
prof_to_depart <- courses_fall_spring |>
  group_by(department, term) |>
  summarise(
    total_prof_depart = n_distinct(instructors)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_prof_depart))

#OUTPUT
prof_to_depart

seats_to_depart <- courses_fall_spring |>
  group_by(department, term) |>
  summarise(
    total_seats_depart = sum(seats)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_seats_depart))

#OUTPUT
seats_to_depart

```

**Q3**: [wildcard] Search the description column for keywords of interest and discuss findings (if a pattern is found, if not keep searching relevant words) 

**A3**: We were curious to see what courses, in which semesters, had the word Trump in their description. We found 10, all of them relevant to the president. Out of the 10 courses mentioning Trump in the data (checked with the out of session semesters), six are journalism courses. The classes started in the spring of 2021, some weeks after the Jan. 6 insurrection at the U.S. capitol. Trump's presidencies has opened doors that severely fractured news production and consumption. So its important to teach future journalists the best tools to navigate the fierce battle to control the flow of information. So, we see these courses, the moment they began and their focus on Trump as a reflection of Philip Merrill's focus on teaching its students real-world journalism.

```{r}
keywords <- c("diversity", "equity", "race", "immigration", "trump", "gender")

chosen_words <- courses_fall_spring |>
  unnest_tokens(word, description) |> 
  filter(word %in% keywords) |>             
  group_by(start_date, word) |>                    
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(count))

#OUTPUT
chosen_words

```

**Q5** 
What school has had the most classes removed as the semesters go by? (Or calculate the percent change from the department
**A5**

There was not one semester that had the same exact courses as another (which makes sense with the winter and summer classes.) While the Business department has the most courses provided with the data frame, it wasn't even on top 20 of the departments with the highest percent change. Departments like University Honors, Physics, and School of Music had an average percent change of courses provided over 1000 percent. While Global Communities, Executive MBA Program, Office of Undergraduate Research had negative average percent change of courses provided throughout semester. 

```{r}
department_ref <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department)) |>
  select(department) |>
  distinct()

department_ref

#classes per semester 

classes_per_department <- umd_courses |>
  separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department)) |>
  group_by(department)|>
  summarize(class_count = n())
  
classes_per_department 


#-- SEMESTERS--# 

#terms ref 
termsem <- umd_courses |>
  select(term) |>
  distinct()|>
  arrange(desc(term))

termsem

#There's 22 terms in this dataset. Should i create a  dataframe that filter each term and group by department to summarize the class count... 22 times OR find a loop code -->  I'll try to create a loop 
   
#trying out loops, trying to remember if the python rules apply
   
#Making a vector with the list of terms I had outputted in previous data set
terms_vector <- unique(termsem$term)
 
#Make an empty list 
results_list_terms <- list()

#Creating loop using the for every term in the term list vector, they will output results...
 
for (term in terms_vector) {
  results <- umd_courses |>
    separate_rows(department, sep = ";") |>
  mutate(department = trimws(department))|>
  filter(term == !!term) |> # the !! forces the code to look at the values under term column as its own dataframe so that the filter can work -- only a tidyverse thing 
  group_by(department)|>
  summarize(class_count = n())
  
  results <- results |> mutate(term = term)
results_list_terms[[as.character(term)]] <-results
}

final_term_list <- bind_rows(results_list_terms,.id = "term")


#Widening the data set so it's easier to read. So that each term is in its own column instead of a part of a terms row. Essentially flipping the data frame  axis
depart_class_termlist  <- final_term_list|>
  pivot_wider(names_from = term, #specifying the unique term semesters are their own column name 
              values_from = class_count, #class_count values will transfer to new columns; under each term
              names_prefix = "term_") 

#Joining the total classes dataframe into the previous one 
depart_class_termlist_2 <- depart_class_termlist |>
  left_join(classes_per_department, by = "department") |>
    rename(
      total_count = class_count 
      #should i rename the term columns? lazy rn no shade. 
    )


#print tibble
depart_class_termlist 
  


avg_percent_change <- depart_class_termlist |>
  select(department, starts_with("term_")) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = starts_with("term_"),  #long format
               names_to = "term", 
               values_to = "class_count") |> 
  group_by(department) |>  
  arrange(term) |>  #  the terms are in order i guess
  mutate(percent_change = (class_count - lag(class_count)) / lag(class_count) * 100) |>  # percent change
  summarise(average_percent_change = mean(percent_change, na.rm = TRUE)) |> 
  ungroup() 


#arrange from high percent change to low
avg_percent_change |>
  arrange(desc(average_percent_change))



```
